summary: This best-practice document sets out a principle that extends the open process principle of RFC 3935. It says there must be a free option for online participation in IETF meetings and, where possible, related IETF-hosted events.

eli5.summary: Anyone should be able to join the big meeting from home for free, not only the people who can pay and travel.

questions: what is the open participation principle
subtitle: The IETF principle that every meeting must offer a free way to take part remotely.

tldr.problem: Fees for remote participation, introduced when meetings went fully online in 2020 and 2021, can be a barrier to both regular and first-time attendees.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets the principle that there must be an option for free remote participation in any IETF meeting, and leaves the implementation details to the IETF LLC.
tldr.outcome: Remote participation need not be free for everyone, but a free option with the same interactivity must always exist and be clearly listed.

facts.label: Core rule
facts.value: A free remote option must exist for any IETF meeting

facts.label: Out of scope
facts.value: In-person participation and the fee structure

today: RFC 9501 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 239) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: How Remote Participation Changed
sections.content:
Remote participation moved from email-only to live chat and audio streaming, and then to a fully online meeting system integrated with the in-room session, with interactive audio and video. It was historically free for remote attendees.

As the option improved, the IETF saw more remote participants, and started to require registration for remote participation, still without a fee. With the move to fully online meetings in 2020 and 2021 there was no distinction between remote and on-site participants, and a meeting fee was charged to remote participants because costs still needed to be covered.

That raised concerns: even a small fee can be a barrier for regular remote attendees and for people considering a first meeting.
sections.eli5: Joining from home used to be free. When everything went online, a fee appeared, and a fee can keep some people out.

sections.title: The Open Participation Principle
sections.content:
The IETF Administration LLC (IETF LLC) is expected to build this principle into its decisions about the remote registration fee structure. The principle: there must be an option for free remote participation in any IETF meeting, regardless of whether the meeting has a physical presence. Related collocated events are encouraged to follow it if they offer remote participation at all.

It extends the open process principle of RFC 3935, which was written mainly with email in mind. Here, openness is to be seen as open and free.

The RFC does not require every meeting to offer remote participation, since there could be technical or other reasons. At a minimum, working group sessions, BoFs and the administrative plenary are expected to provide it.
sections.eli5: The rule: if people can join online at all, there has to be a free way to do it.

sections.title: What the Free Option Must Look Like
sections.content:
The RFC leaves implementation to the LLC. At the time of publication, a request for a fee waiver was the approach implemented.

  • The free option must offer the same interactivity and functionality as paid remote participation, and it must not be possible to identify participants who used it.
  • Extra services beyond regular registration may still be offered for a charge. The LLC should consider whether to offer them free to those in need.
  • The free option must be clearly and prominently listed on the meeting website and registration page, and any extra steps, such as applying for a waiver, should be clearly documented.
  • Personal information collected about use of the free option must be kept confidential.
sections.eli5: The free seat must be just as good as a paid seat, and nobody should be able to tell who sat in it.

sections.title: Financial Impact and the LLC's Role
sections.content:
The RFC does not aim to make remote participation free for everyone. Meeting fees help distribute operating costs, though they do not fully offset the cost of the meeting or the IETF. The principle applies only to remote participation. In-person participation and changes to the fee structure or funding model are out of scope.

Under RFC 8711, the LLC manages the IETF's finances. If unlimited free participation is found to harm financial sustainability, the LLC is expected to implement measures to manage costs. The RFC does not restrict it. The LLC should share its decision and rationale, consider community consultation under Section 4.4 of RFC 8711, and describe the process in enough detail for participants to make an informed choice.

Any limit on free registrations likely needs an eligibility assessment, which is difficult and can cause unfairness and hurt openness, so that should be weighed seriously.
sections.eli5: The people who run the money may add rules if too many free seats become a problem, but they must explain why.

sections.title: Use and Misuse of the Free Option
sections.content:
The RFC sets no rules on who should use the free option. It cannot be limited to a group such as students or self-funded participants, nor by number of meetings attended or previous involvement.

Participants whose sponsors can pay are expected to use paid registration, which supports the IETF's sustainability. The LLC should monitor trends and publish aggregated data on the number and percentage of free registrations, without revealing personal information.

A rise in free registrations is a success, likely a sign of increased interest rather than misuse, and should not be linked to the number of paid registrations. Paid registrations may fall for other reasons, such as travel restrictions, cost savings or loss of business interest.
sections.eli5: If more people use the free seats, that is good news: more people are interested.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it introduces no new concerns for the security of Internet protocols, and it has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: This is a rule about meetings, not about computers, so it does not change how anything is kept safe.

references.text: Alvestrand, H., "A Mission Statement for the IETF", BCP 95, RFC 3935, October 2004.
Haberman, B., Hall, J., and J. Livingood, "Structure of the IETF Administrative Support Activity, Version 2.0", BCP 101, RFC 8711, February 2020.
